bread-lard-puerto-rican-style.title: Bread with Lard, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Bread with lard in Puerto Rican style is a traditional snack consisting of soft white bread soaked in flavorful pork lard seasoned with typical Puerto Rican spices such as adobo, oregano, and garlic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Puerto Rico in the early 20th century when Spanish colonists adapted local recipes using readily available pork lard.
The lard is often rendered until golden, giving the bread a crisp, buttery crust.
It is traditionally served with “mojo” sauce – a spicy tomato‑pepper sauce.
In Puerto Rico it is commonly eaten for breakfast or as a bar snack with beer.
Lard is considered an energy‑dense food and is often consumed during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: High energy source
items.content: Lard provides a large amount of calories, quickly replenishing energy stores.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 in pork lard is essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Fatty acids for satiety
items.content: Saturated and monounsaturated fats in lard can promote a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Aids fat‑soluble vitamin absorption
items.content: The fats help absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K from other foods.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Overconsumption may lead to weight gain.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Frequent intake can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Lard is often salted; people with hypertension should limit portions.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to pork proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bread is usually served warm, sliced. It can be spread on toast, added to sandwiches, or used as a base for toppings like mojo sauce, avocado, or fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in an airtight container for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag where it retains flavor for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven or skillet before serving.

cabbage-green-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-to-.title: Cabbage, green, cooked, fat added, NS

content.title: About
content.content: Green cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata) is a leafy vegetable widely used in cooking. When boiled with added fat (oil, butter, or other vegetable fats) it becomes tender and gains a richer flavor. The product is classified as NS (non‑specific) regarding fat type.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cabbage is a rich source of vitamin C, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.
Glucosinolates in cabbage aid the body’s detoxification processes.
In traditional Russian cuisine cabbage is often boiled with butter or sour cream to enhance taste and absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Fresh cabbage can be stored in the refrigerator for up to two weeks in an airtight container.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in cabbage promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Adding fat enhances the bioavailability of vitamins A, D, E, and K.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A serving of cooked cabbage with a modest amount of fat provides about 70 kcal.

items.title: Sensitivity to glucosinolates
items.content: Large amounts may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in some individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When salt is added, monitor overall sodium intake.

items.title: Cabbage allergy
items.content: Rare, but possible allergic reactions in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil cabbage in salted water, then stir in butter or vegetable oil, season with salt and herbs. Serve as a side dish, in soups, or incorporate into casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cabbage in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Candy Licorice (item 5105) are sweets made from licorice extract, sugar and glucose syrup. They feature a distinctive mildly bitter flavor with hints of anise and sweet caramel, and their texture ranges from chewy to hard depending on the recipe.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Licorice was originally used in medicine as a remedy for coughs and colds.
It is believed that licorice root was known already in ancient Egypt.
In some countries, such as Finland, licorice candies are considered a national treat.
The glycyrrhizin content gives licorice a slightly sweet after‑taste that is perceived differently across cultures.
Mass production of licorice sweets began in Europe in the 19th century after extraction methods were refined.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Licorice extract has traditionally been used to soothe heartburn and stomach discomfort.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Polyphenols present in licorice provide a modest antioxidant activity.

items.title: Calming aroma
items.content: Anise flavor, often added to licorice candies, can have a mild soothing effect.

items.title: Blood pressure increase
items.content: High amounts of glycyrrhizin may cause sodium retention and raise blood pressure in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to ingredients such as flavorings or colorants.

items.title: Dental caries
items.content: The sugar content promotes tooth decay when consumed frequently.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candy Licorice can be enjoyed as a snack, added to dessert mixes, used in baking, or as a garnish for cocktails. It is advisable not to overconsume to avoid excess sugar and glycyrrhizin intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the candies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent melting and texture changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey cooked in teriyaki sauce is tender meat coated with a sweet‑salty aromatic sauce made from soy sauce, sugar, ginger and garlic. The dish is popular in Asian cuisine and is often served with rice or vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teriyaki comes from the Japanese word meaning “to grill” or “to broil”.
Traditional teriyaki sauce is made from soy sauce, mirin, sugar and sometimes sake.
Chicken teriyaki is common in fast‑food and ready‑meal products, while turkey is chosen for lower‑fat options.
The dish gained worldwide popularity thanks to American fast‑food chains.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Skinless meat contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Sources of selenium, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of the sauce
items.content: Ginger and garlic in teriyaki have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant effects.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce in teriyaki is salty and can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Traditional teriyaki sauce is sweet; people monitoring blood sugar should limit portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy sauce.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Choose fresh, minimally processed meat to avoid the risk of foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot with steamed rice, noodles, or vegetable sides, or slice it for salads. Cut the meat into thin strips, stir‑fry quickly over high heat, then coat with teriyaki sauce and lightly caramelize.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chicken or turkey with teriyaki in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Brewed coffee made from ground beans (Coffea arabica or C. robusta) is a popular beverage containing caffeine, aromatic compounds, and antioxidants. Brewing releases its characteristic aroma, a slightly bitter taste, and a stimulating effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coffee is the second most consumed drink in the world after water.
The first documented method of brewing coffee appeared in the 15th century in Yemen.
There are over 100 coffee varieties, but more than 60 % of global production comes from Arabica.
Caffeine in coffee stimulates the central nervous system, enhancing alertness.
Coffee can be prepared in many ways: espresso, drip, French press, Turkish, and more.

items.title: Boosts alertness
items.content: Caffeine raises adrenaline levels, improving concentration and reaction time.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is high in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Caffeine may increase metabolic rate and aid fat burning.

items.title: May lower risk of certain diseases
items.content: Moderate coffee consumption is linked to reduced risk of Parkinson’s disease, type‑2 diabetes, and some cancers.

items.title: Improves mood
items.content: Caffeine stimulates dopamine and serotonin production, which can lift mood.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after coffee.

items.title: Blood pressure increase
items.content: High doses of caffeine can temporarily raise blood pressure, important for hypertensive persons.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can irritate the stomach and cause heartburn in people with high gastric acidity.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain medications, such as CNS stimulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coffee is usually served hot, but it can be cooled and made into iced coffee. Milk, cream, sugar, syrups, or spices are added to taste. For a milder flavor, use a coarser grind and shorter brew time.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dark place, preferably in the refrigerator, to preserve aroma. Avoid prolonged exposure to air, moisture, and light, as they accelerate oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Flavored half‑and‑half cream is a blend of equal parts cream and milk enriched with natural flavorings. It has a smooth, buttery taste with a subtle hint of the chosen flavor (vanilla, strawberry, caramel, etc.) and is used as an additive for coffee, desserts, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of cream and milk gives a softer texture than straight cream.
Flavorings are often derived from natural extracts, though artificial components may also be used.
The product is a staple in cafés for preparing lattes and cappuccinos.
In some countries “half and half” is classified as a distinct dairy product with its own regulations.
Typical fat content is around 10‑12 %.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Both cream and milk provide calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains vitamins B2 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Milk protein contributes to muscle maintenance.

items.title: Flavor enhancement
items.content: Flavored half‑and‑half adds aroma to drinks and desserts without extra sugar.

items.title: Easier digestion
items.content: The lower fat content compared to pure cream makes it easier to digest.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to this product.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Although lower than straight cream, it is still calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: Some flavorings may be artificial; check the label if you are sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add flavored half‑and‑half to coffee, hot chocolate, sauces, soups, purees, or use it in baking and desserts as a lighter alternative to pure cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 1‑4 °C in the original container. Once opened, use within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato sauce is a ready‑to‑heat meal that stays refrigerated and only needs warming. The combination of al dente pasta and a fragrant tomato sauce seasoned with basil, oregano, and garlic provides a balanced flavor. Perfect for a quick lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce is made from ripe tomatoes, which are rich in lycopene – a powerful antioxidant.
The pasta used is typically durum wheat, giving it a firm texture after heating.
The product is often sold in single‑serve packages, making calorie control easy.
Traditional tomato sauce includes olive oil, which enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Microwave heating preserves most nutrients when the recommended time is not exceeded.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes supports heart health and has anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Pasta provides sustained energy through slow‑release glucose.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sauce and pasta contain B1, B3 and B6, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Ready‑to‑heat versions usually contain little added fat unless extra oil is added.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Tomatoes and whole‑grain pasta contribute fiber that aids normal bowel function.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared meals can be high in salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat pasta contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain preservatives for shelf life; choose additive‑free options if sensitive.

items.title: Overheating
items.content: Excessive heating can degrade pasta texture and create a bitter taste.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in a microwave or on the stovetop according to package directions (usually 2–3 minutes). For extra flavor, sprinkle grated Parmesan, add fresh basil, or drizzle a little olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑4 days. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
